blogs.title: How to Choose an Industrial EPC Contractor
blogs.excerpt: Learn key criteria and strategic guidelines for selecting the right industrial EPC contractor for your plant, factory, or processing facility to ensure timely delivery and operational excellence.
blogs.content:
When you plan a plant, a factory, or a large processing facility, the first big decision that you will have to make is neither the machinery nor the location but how to choose an EPC contractor  to make your drawings and budget come alive into a facility that works. Do it correctly and you will feel like the entire project was a boring experience, in a good way. Do it incorrectly and you will spend two years running around delay claims, change orders, and finger pointing.
The following guidelines are meant for those who are responsible for selecting an EPC industrial contractor. We have tried to keep it very practical. Ten points, along with the things that you need to ask, see and avoid.

What Does an Industrial EPC Contractor Actually Do?

EPC is an acronym for Engineering, Procurement and Construction. The right EPC contractor will assume complete responsibility for the entire project, which involves engineering and design, procurement and delivery of equipment and material, construction on site, and commissioning of the plant. There is one responsible party to work with instead of five or six.
The entire value lies in that complete responsibility. That is also the reason why the selection of an EPC contractor should receive much more attention than what most organizations do. The turnkey contract carries a great deal of risk, and only the competent and financially sound organization can handle it.

Why EPC Contractor Selection Goes Wrong

Most bad outcomes trace back to the same three habits. Owners compare only the headline price. They trust a polished presentation over site evidence. And they sign before the scope is properly defined. Keep those three in mind as you read the checklist below, because every point is really a way of avoiding them.

How to Choose an EPC Contractor: The 10-Point Evaluation Guide

1. Examine the Industrial EPC Contractor's Experience
Length of time in business is not an important factor. What counts is whether the EPC contractor has done anything similar to your project in terms of industry, size and complexity. Even though a company has completed ten warehouses, it might have trouble completing a chemical plant or heavy fabrication facility.
Get a list of projects, including capacity, contract amount, location and completion date. Then, find out which project is most like yours and why.

2. Check the On-Time Delivery Record
Promising a schedule is easy. Find out the real deal: how many projects did they deliver on time? Why were some delayed? A good industrial EPC contractor will talk about this openly and tell you what changes they made after the delay.
Contact at least three former clients, and make sure one of them is a project that was problematic for the contractor.

3. Scrutinize Safety Performance
Safety performance is not something you can document on paper. It manifests itself in costs, productivity, and legal liability. Get the contractor's lost-time injury frequency rate, the site safety plan, and certifications like ISO 45001. And if possible, go to an active site and observe – are workers using harnesses when working at heights, is scaffolding tagged, are permits being complied with?
A contractor with poor safety performance will most likely have poor site discipline.

4. Assess the Engineering Capability
The "E" in EPC is where cost and quality decisions are made behind the scenes. In-house engineering capability translates into better designs, less clash risk on site, and better materials selection. Find out who does the detailed engineering, whether it is in-house or outsourced, and what tools and procedures they employ.
Spend time with the chief engineers rather than the salespeople. Let them walk you through the process of solving one difficult aspect of your design. You'll learn a lot in ten minutes.

5. Know How They Control Cost
A cheap bid does not necessarily mean a cheap project. You should learn how the EPC contractor prepares his estimate, what is included and excluded from it, how he handles contingency, and how he controls variations. The good contractor will be able to demonstrate how the cost can be broken down and how value engineering can help you cut costs without sacrificing quality.
Be careful with a quote that is significantly lower than others. It most likely means that some scope was left out and you will pay for it through change orders.

6. Evaluate Procurement Capability
Procurement is where many projects lose several months. An experienced industrial EPC contractor has solid relationships with vendors, a reliable list of suppliers, and a proper procedure of inspection and expediting. Ask how the contractor manages long lead materials such as transformers, large motors, or structural steel, and how he reacts to the failure of a supplier to meet the deadline.
Good procurement helps you preserve quality as well.

7. Review Construction and Site Management
A good plan on paper is worth very little without competent people to put it into practice. Examine the proposed project management team: project manager, planning engineer, safety officer, and quality officer. Examine their experience and, most critically, whether they will be available for your project or diverted to some other assignment.
Ask to see a sample project schedule and progress report. Competent contractors use critical path scheduling and issue weekly progress reports including photos and explanations of any variances.

8. Examine the Contractor’s Financial Standing
Turnkey contractors finance a lot of work upfront prior to payment. Poor financial standing results in suppliers refusing to ship and employees refusing to show up for work. Request audited financial statements from the past three years, their order book, and their banking connections. Make sure that they have the capability of issuing performance and advance payment guarantees from banks.
An EPC contractor in good financial standing is one that can withstand a bad month without endangering your project.

9. Review the Contract Terms and Risk Management
The contract turns promises into obligations. Consider the issues of scope definition, payment milestones, delay liquidated damages, performance guarantee, warranty period and dispute resolution. FIDIC type contracts are popular for the reasons mentioned above.
It is important to involve your legal department from the very beginning. A contractor who welcomes examination of the terms is a contractor who is sure about their capability to deliver.

10. Clarify Commissioning, Handover and Post-Handover Support
There is still much to be done after the construction works are completed. Find out how the EPC contractor commissions the facility, trains the operator, prepares documentation and as-built drawings. And then find out what will happen during the first year after the handover. Whom should you contact at 2 a.m. in case of a problem?
A proper defects liability procedure and availability of post-handover support are a sign of a reliable contractor.

Quick Scorecard for EPC Contractor Selection
Use a simple weighted score so the decision is not driven by gut feeling alone.
Criteria
Suggested weight
Relevant industrial experience
15%
Delivery track record
15%
Safety performance
10%
Engineering depth
15%
Cost transparency
15%
Procurement and site management
10%
Financial strength
10%
Contract terms and after-sales
10%


Adjust the weights to suit your project. A time-critical build might weigh delivery higher; a complex process plant might weigh engineering higher.

Red Flags When You Choose an EPC Contractor
An offer significantly below all other quotes without any explanation.
Resistance to allow site visits and/or references from previous customers.
Ambiguous scope or too many “by owner” items.
Different team members show up after the contract is signed.
Urgency to sign now.
If you see two or more of these, proceed with caution.

Common Mistakes Owners Make
The first one is beginning the process of selecting EPC contractors before the fundamental requirements are finalized. Determine capacity, layout, utilities, and quality standards first. The second one is basing the choice on price. The third one is failing to consider the cultural fit because you will be working very closely with this group of people for quite a long time.

Final Thoughts
Knowing how to select an EPC contractor depends on facts rather than promises: relevant experience, proven delivery, good safety and engineering, realistic costing, and proper contract. Go through these ten points, score your shortlist, and discuss it with real customers.
At PISL, we deliver industrial projects the way we would like to see them delivered ourselves: well-defined scope of works, realistic costs, and no surprises. If you have an industrial EPC contractor shortlist and want to discuss your project, contact our team and we will walk you through our approach to it.

# Industrial Flooring Options for Manufacturing Plants

Choosing flooring is typically the final task in planning a factory project, which is precisely why it can become problematic. At the point when the decision is made, the structure has already been determined, along with any slope requirements and curing times, even though the floor may be the most heavily trafficked area in the building.

**Industrial flooring for factories cannot be merely a cosmetic choice; it is a decision about structural integrity and safety compliance that must be addressed alongside the project's civil engineering.**

The floor of a factory has to be able to handle forklift traffic, chemical spills, machine vibration, temperature fluctuations, and constant foot traffic for 10 years or more without being replaced.

# Why This Decision Belongs Earlier in the Project

The flooring is not an independent finishing but is linked with the sub-base, drainage system, expansion joints, and the curing period of the entire building.

Selecting the **industrial flooring for factories** in conjunction with the total EPC and civil work scope, rather than as an add-on at the end, will ensure that the sub-base is properly compacted, the moisture barrier is properly laid, and time for curing is factored into the schedule.

The floors hurriedly done to meet the deadline are the ones that develop cracks and delamination within a year.

# The Major Flooring Types Used in Manufacturing

# Epoxy Resin Flooring

Epoxy resin flooring is one of the most widely used flooring types in manufacturing. Epoxy resin can be installed on concrete as a seamless flooring system, providing good chemical resistance, easy maintenance, and durability.

![industrial flooring for factories.avif](/images/blogs/industrial_flooring_for_factories_32e837e8a8.avif)

This type of flooring is suitable for areas such as automotive assembly shops, food processing facilities, and pharmaceutical plants where chemical resistance and cleanliness are required.

A disadvantage of epoxy resin flooring is the time-consuming application and proper substrate preparation; otherwise, the epoxy will peel off within a few months.

# Polished and Hardened Concrete

Polished and hardened concrete is a relatively economical material that provides a very durable floor, suitable for heavy manufacturing and warehouse applications.

First, the concrete floor is treated with hardening compounds, then it is polished. Polishing and hardening of concrete result in an abrasion-resistant, dense floor suitable for the movement of forklifts and heavy equipment.

This type of flooring is less resistant to chemicals than epoxy resin flooring.

# Vitrified and Anti-Skid Tiles

Vitrified and anti-skid tiles are suitable where hygiene, aesthetic appearance, and non-slip characteristics need to be combined, such as in quality control laboratories, packing zones, and staff zones.

They are more costly to install and maintain than poured systems and are not commonly used on the production line itself, although there are justifiable reasons for their use in particular zones.

# Anti-Static Flooring

Anti-static flooring is a specialised flooring system designed for electronics manufacturing and situations where static discharge could damage equipment components or pose a fire risk.

It has conductive components that allow dissipation of static charge and is important in facilities where electronics or certain chemical processes are manufactured.

# Heavy-Duty Industrial Screed

A heavy-duty industrial screed is installed in areas requiring high point loads or machinery bases.

This type of flooring is often installed in heavy engineering plants and facilities such as copper smelting plants.

# Matching Flooring to the Actual Use Case

It’s less a matter of preference than it is about what the floor has to endure daily.

For high-load and forklift traffic, polished concrete or a reinforced screed is better suited than coated flooring because it can withstand impact without damaging the surface.

For chemical exposure and food-grade standards, epoxy resin flooring is often preferred because it is seamless, non-porous, and resistant to cleaning chemicals and oily or acidic substances.

Anti-static flooring is essential where controlling electrostatic discharge is a critical requirement, such as electronics manufacturing.

None of these options need to be mutually exclusive in one facility.

It is not unusual for a plant to use epoxy flooring in its production areas, hardened concrete in its warehousing areas, and anti-static flooring in the electronics assembly area all in the same building.

# Where Cross-Sector Experience Matters

Industrial flooring requirements differ greatly from industry to industry, and a contractor with experience working only within one industry may apply the same specification regardless of its suitability.

PISL has delivered more than 16 million square feet of industrial infrastructure since 2009, across sectors including automotive, warehousing, heavy engineering, industrial manufacturing, food processing, and copper smelting.

This cross-sector experience covers a wide range of industrial flooring requirements, from hygiene-focused flooring in food processing plants to heavy-duty floors for engineering applications.

There is no one-size-fits-all industrial factory floor specification.

While a particular flooring specification may be suitable for warehousing, the same solution may be inappropriate for food processing or electronics manufacturing.

# Planning Flooring as Part of the Bigger Picture

One of the most easily prevented mistakes in industrial construction is treating flooring in factory buildings as an afterthought.

Correcting a failed floor can involve partial demolition and refitting while the manufacturing process is ongoing.

Planning the industrial flooring system in parallel with the other civil and structural components, based on the actual load and hygiene needs of the facility from the beginning, is clearly the more economical and efficient approach.

When designing a new manufacturing facility or replacing flooring in an existing one, the PISL team can help determine which industrial flooring specification best suits your industry's loads, operational requirements and compliance needs as part of the broader facility design.

# Choosing the Right Industrial Construction Partner: 12 Questions to Ask

Choosing an **industrial construction company** will be one of the hardest decisions, and it is difficult to undo once construction has started.

Whereas in most business deals you are able to switch vendors midway without too much hassle, that is not the case when it comes to industrial construction, where, once started, you may face significant costs through delays, rework, contractual changes and disruption.

This makes the pre-contract evaluation process more valuable than simply comparing the lowest bids that arrive in your mailbox.

The typical buyer will consider price and delivery timeframe, but the following questions go beyond that basic process. They should be part of the evaluation list you use when assessing industrial construction companies.

# 1. Do You Have Direct Experience in Our Sector?

A building designed for food processing has unique hygienic and compliance requirements compared with a building designed for heavy engineering or automobile production.

![Choosing the Right Industrial Construction Partner 12 Questions to Ask.avif](/images/blogs/Choosing_the_Right_Industrial_Construction_Partner_12_Questions_to_Ask_284223dc16.avif)

Ask the contractor to provide real-world examples from your own industry. A good response should include relevant project examples along with the challenges encountered and solutions implemented.

Relevant experience demonstrates that the contractor understands the technical, regulatory and operational requirements of your industry before construction begins.

# 2. Are You Providing Single-Point Responsibility, or Do We Need to Coordinate Several Vendors?

This question can help identify risks associated with fragmented project delivery.

An industrial construction company providing integrated engineering, procurement and construction can take responsibility across the major project stages rather than requiring the client to coordinate several independent vendors.

Single-point accountability can simplify communication, reduce coordination gaps and make it clearer who is responsible when technical or execution issues arise.

# 3. What Is Your Safety and HSE Record?

Safety should be evaluated through actual performance rather than statements in a proposal.

Find out about the company's safety record, relevant certifications, incident-management processes and how HSE procedures are implemented at project sites.

You should be cautious about a contractor that cannot provide specific information about safety performance, even if the commercial proposal appears attractive.

# 4. What Is Your Value Engineering Procedure?

Value engineering should reduce unnecessary lifecycle costs without compromising performance, safety or quality.

Ask how the contractor evaluates different materials, systems, equipment specifications and structural solutions before construction begins.

A strong value-engineering process should demonstrate how design decisions are assessed against performance, cost, maintenance and long-term operational requirements.

# 5. Have There Been Any Timeline Delays, and If Yes, How Did You Handle Them?

Every industrial construction contractor may face project challenges or delays.

The important question is how those situations were identified, managed and addressed.

A contractor that openly explains the causes of previous delays and the corrective actions taken can provide more meaningful insight than one that simply claims a perfect record.

Look for evidence of structured planning, risk management and lessons learned.

# 6. How Much Work Is Performed In-House Versus Through Subcontractors?

Ask which project activities are managed directly by the contractor and which are subcontracted.

Understanding the balance between in-house capabilities and subcontracted work can help you evaluate the contractor's control over engineering, civil, structural, mechanical, electrical and other critical scopes.

More direct control over critical activities can help improve coordination, quality and schedule management, depending on the project's delivery structure.

# 7. How Is Your Quality Control Conducted?

Ask what inspections are carried out, what material testing procedures are followed and whether third-party quality audits are used where appropriate.

A professional contractor should be able to explain its inspection and testing processes clearly.

Quality control should be documented, measurable and consistently implemented throughout the project rather than dependent on individual site teams.

# 8. What Is Your Philosophy Regarding Sustainability and Energy Efficiency?

Sustainability goes beyond environmental impact. It can directly influence the operating cost and performance of an industrial facility throughout its lifecycle.

Ask how energy efficiency, resource efficiency, sustainable materials, water management and other relevant considerations are incorporated into the standard design and construction process.

The strongest approach is to treat sustainability as part of the project strategy rather than simply an optional upgrade.

# 9. What Assistance Do You Provide After Completion?

A building does not stop requiring attention after construction or commissioning.

Ask about post-completion support, warranty coverage, response timelines for defects and whether the same project team or organisation can support maintenance and corrective work after handover.

Clear post-completion responsibilities can provide additional confidence during the operational phase of the facility.

# 10. Do You Have Financial Stability for a Long-Term Project?

It may feel uncomfortable to ask directly, but financial stability is an important consideration for large-scale and long-duration projects.

Review the company's experience with projects of comparable size and duration and understand how long it has been operating in the industry.

The objective is to assess whether the contractor has the organisational and financial capacity to remain reliable throughout the project lifecycle.

# 11. Can You Provide Former Client References and Site Visits?

References and site visits can provide much more insight than simply reviewing a portfolio.

Ask whether you can speak with previous clients and, where appropriate, visit completed projects.

A confident industrial construction company should be able to demonstrate its previous work and provide evidence of how its facilities perform after completion.

# 12. How Are Scope Changes Handled During the Project?

Scope changes occur in many industrial projects for reasons including regulatory requirements, site conditions, design development and changing business needs.

Before signing the contract, understand how changes will be evaluated, priced, approved and incorporated into the project schedule.

A clearly defined change-management process can help reduce misunderstandings and unexpected commercial disputes during construction.

# What Good Answers Tend to Have in Common

Good responses to the questions above share several characteristics: they are specific, transparent and supported by evidence rather than guarantees.

A contractor that confidently responds to every question but cannot provide supporting documentation is providing limited value.

By contrast, a contractor that openly discusses challenges from previous projects and explains the changes made afterwards can demonstrate a stronger culture of accountability and continuous improvement.

Pragati Infra Solutions Limited (PISL) has developed more than 16 million square feet of industrial infrastructure since 2009 across automotive, warehousing, heavy engineering, industrial manufacturing, food processing and copper smelting projects.

With a workforce of more than 600 professionals and an integrated engineering, procurement and construction structure, PISL brings multidisciplinary capabilities to industrial infrastructure projects.

The company's MoU with AG&P Industrial to establish an advanced modular EPC and fabrication facility in Andhra Pradesh further reflects its focus on engineered, scalable and future-ready industrial infrastructure.

# A Note on How to Use This List in Practice

Do not view these twelve questions as a one-shot exercise to be completed in a single meeting and then forgotten.

Ideally, ask all shortlisted industrial construction companies the same questions and compare their responses side by side.

Verbal reassurances can sound convincing until work begins. That is why it is advisable to request important commitments, assumptions and project responsibilities in writing wherever possible.

Also pay attention to information that contractors provide without being asked.

An industrial construction company that openly discusses previous project challenges, explains how its processes have improved and offers relevant site visits without being prompted may be demonstrating a higher level of transparency.

Answers that remain vague despite repeated clarification should not be ignored.

# The Right Questions Lead to the Right Partner

Selecting an industrial construction company is ultimately about more than choosing a quotation.

The right partner should demonstrate relevant sector experience, technical capability, safety performance, quality systems, transparent communication, financial stability and the ability to manage the complete project lifecycle.

When looking for an industrial construction partner for your next project, the PISL team is ready to discuss these twelve questions and explain how its integrated EPC capabilities can be applied to your specific facility and industry requirements.

# Factory Expansion Checklist Before Starting Civil Construction

The vast majority of factory expansion delays do not arise on the building site itself. They occur weeks earlier, during the period when a company approves the civil works before the foundation works, both figurative and literal, have been done.

By the time the first foundation pour occurs, many of the factors which would later cause a significant delay have already been predetermined, and there is nothing that can be done about them on-site at that point.

But before hiring an **industrial construction company** to start pouring foundations, some things need to be sorted out first.

# Site and Soil Assessment

Each expansion plan must begin with a thorough geotechnical survey of the land, not with assumptions based on soil conditions at the plant's present location.

![pisl.avif](/images/blogs/pisl_1889ae287f.avif)

Soil a few hundred metres from the current plot can be totally different in terms of its behaviour under load, compaction, depth of the water table and other factors. Omitting this step is one of the frequent causes of foundation redesign, which is costly and inefficient because it is quite avoidable.

In addition to the soil conditions, it is necessary to take into account the presence of drainage on the land and the possibility of flooding due to the seasonal rise of the water table level.

The floor of the factory may seem perfectly dry and ready for laying foundations in dry weather but may turn out to be a puddle during the period of monsoon rains.

That is why such a check should be carried out professionally and not visually, especially since a visual assessment may take place during a favourable weather period.

# Regulatory and Statutory Approvals

Any factory expansion project may require approvals for environmental clearance, fire safety NOC, building plans, labour department clearance and other permissions, depending on the state and sector involved.

One of the quickest ways of finding oneself with a partially constructed factory is initiating civil work without the required approvals in place.

An experienced **industrial construction company** understands which approvals need to be addressed during the early design stage and which permissions can prevent construction from proceeding.

These requirements should therefore be mapped before the construction schedule is finalised. This allows realistic timelines to be established based on actual approval requirements rather than assumptions.

# Utility and Infrastructure Capacity

A factory expansion imposes additional load on the power, water and effluent infrastructure that was initially built to handle the needs of the original facility.

Before construction, confirm that there will be sufficient electrical capacity and determine whether a substation upgrade is required.

Water availability and effluent-handling capacity should also be evaluated against the increased production and building footprint.

You certainly don't want to discover a capacity constraint after the building is complete. Adding infrastructure to a completed facility is generally more difficult and disruptive than planning the required capacity before construction begins.

# Budget and Contingency Planning

A realistic expansion budget goes beyond the basic construction cost.

Fluctuations in material prices, statutory fees, utility upgrades and unforeseen site conditions should all be considered at the outset.

An initial contingency allowance of around 10–15% can provide a buffer for project-specific uncertainties, although the appropriate amount should be determined based on the scope, location and risk profile of the project.

Projects without contingency planning can come to a halt when unexpected expenses arise because there is no allowance available within the approved budget.

A reliable **industrial construction company** should provide a detailed breakdown of where contingency costs may arise on a particular project rather than simply presenting a single unexplained contingency figure.

# Timeline Realism

Request a construction schedule that takes into account approval timelines, monsoon or seasonal working windows, procurement lead times and specialised equipment delivery rather than construction time alone.

A schedule that considers only the physical construction period is typically the first to go out of the window.

This can become a source of disputes between a company and its contractor even when the contractor is technically meeting the construction milestones that were originally defined.

An **industrial construction company** should ideally be involved before site plans are fully completed so that construction requirements, procurement timelines and execution constraints can be incorporated into the planning process.

Early involvement creates more realistic expectations around project timelines.

# Choosing the Right Construction Partner

This is the decision that will determine whether the rest of this checklist is addressed properly or not.

Try to identify an **industrial construction company** that has previous experience working in the same or similar industry.

A plant designed for food processing has different compliance and hygienic requirements from a plant used for heavy engineering or copper smelting.

A construction firm without relevant industry experience may have to develop its understanding of those requirements during the project, increasing the risk of avoidable coordination issues.

Pragati Infra Solutions Limited (PISL) has completed more than 16 million square feet of industrial infrastructure since 2009, with experience across industries including automotive, warehousing, heavy engineering, industrial manufacturing, food processing and copper smelting.

This experience is valuable because industrial facilities cannot always be developed using the same formula. Different production environments create different requirements for structure, utilities, safety, materials, logistics and execution.

# Safety and Compliance Planning

Finally, validate how the contractor intends to actively manage construction-site safety, particularly when the expansion is taking place adjacent to an existing operating plant.

HSE requirements, access control, material movement and coordination between construction activities and existing plant operations should all be settled before construction begins.

This is particularly important when the existing plant continues operating alongside the expansion.

Poorly managed construction activities can create hazardous situations for construction workers and existing plant personnel while potentially disrupting ongoing production.

When construction is being carried out adjacent to an existing plant, verify whether the contractor has sufficient experience managing live-site operations.

A live industrial site is fundamentally different from an empty construction site because construction activities must be coordinated with ongoing production, access requirements, safety controls and operational constraints.

# Factory Expansion Checklist Before Civil Construction

Before starting civil construction, confirm the following:

- Geotechnical and soil investigation completed
- Drainage and water-table conditions assessed
- Required statutory approvals identified and planned
- Fire and environmental requirements reviewed
- Electrical capacity verified
- Water and effluent capacity checked
- Utility upgrades identified
- Project budget reviewed
- Contingency allowance established
- Procurement and equipment lead times considered
- Monsoon and seasonal constraints considered
- Construction schedule reviewed
- Contractor's relevant industry experience verified
- HSE and access-control plan prepared
- Live-site coordination requirements established

# Where to Go From Here

There is no need to work this out alone.

A good **industrial construction company** should go through this checklist with you before the project begins rather than waiting for issues to appear during construction.

A realistic contingency allowance, early involvement of the right construction partner and proper planning of site, utilities, approvals and safety requirements can make a significant difference to the success of a factory expansion.

If you are planning an industrial factory expansion, the team at Pragati Infra Solutions Limited can help you evaluate the construction requirements and develop a realistic execution approach around your operational needs.

# How Industrial EPC Projects Reduce Long-Term Operational Costs

The buying process that many industrial clients use to purchase their industrial EPC contractors is akin to how they would buy a car; the cheapest car always wins the race. The difference, however, is that a building isn't a five-year-old item. It's a twenty-year-old item. Moreover, the design and construction choices will set your operation costs for each year of the next twenty years.

![industrial EPC contractor.avif](/images/blogs/industrial_EPC_contractor_83969ef29f.avif)

The dialogue that PISL engages in with the plant managers and CFOs today is more frequent than it was five years ago; it is no longer "How much will this cost to build?" but "How much will this cost to operate?"

# Why the Build Price Is the Wrong Number to Anchor On

Lower-cost construction implies lower-cost materials such as thinner insulation, an undersized heating, ventilation, and air conditioning system, lower-quality lighting, and equipment that was selected to save money in its purchase price but which will have no relation to cycle-efficiency.

All these do not appear on the original invoice. The cost appears eighteen months later in the form of a 20% higher utility bill, or unexpected machine downtime due to poor design and engineering without regard to maintenance issues. This becomes apparent only when the damage has been done by the time the contractor has left and the business bears the brunt of it.

The veteran **industrial EPC contractor** views the build cost as merely a single factor of a much longer cost formula, not as the sole cost formula. It is this very difference between transactional provider and true delivery partner that can be detected in the contractor’s approach to the project even prior to its start.

# Where the Real Savings Get Engineered In

Single point accountability is the first lever, and it is also one that many people tend to underestimate the most.

With one industrial EPC contractor responsible for engineering, procurement, and construction from start to finish, nobody can blame each other for systems not being compatible between the electrical subcontractor and the HVAC supplier.

This type of delivery PISL has employed consistently in sectors as diverse as the automotive industry, food processing plants, and the copper smelting industries, all of which have strict tolerance levels, leaving virtually no room for design compromises to arise later in expensive fixes.

The fragmented delivery model does just that: it optimises each individual element on its own.

The second is value engineering, which is frequently misinterpreted as “taking shortcuts.” When applied effectively, it involves evaluating different materials, structures, and equipment specifications before starting construction so that the facility will be appropriately scaled to its load requirements without being overbuilt in some areas and underbuilt in others.

That’s where many potential sources of future energy and maintenance inefficiency get weeded out at low cost while still on the drawing board, not identified and rectified at high cost down the road.

The third is energy-efficient design, which becomes more important all the time. High building envelope efficiency, HVAC sizing based on accurate thermal loads, and advanced lighting systems are no longer optional features; they become required specifications in any professional industrial project because energy remains one of the biggest operating expenses in a facility.

Another one that may go unrecognised when designing the facility is the need to design for ease of maintenance, not just for the initial commissioning. Designing the facility with access to the equipment and scheduled maintenance will ensure that your facility does not suffer from lost revenue through equipment downtime and costly repairs in the coming years.

If it is easy to maintain, then it will be maintained.

# The Industry Is Already Moving in This Direction

It’s not just a philosophy limited to the concept of PISL but rather an approach that the entire EPC industry is looking forward to adopting.

In terms of evaluating a contractor, it’s no longer about the contractor’s capability of constructing at a higher rate; instead, what is being evaluated is the contractor’s ability to incorporate digitalisation, sustainability, and value engineering during the design phase of the project.

The strategy adopted by PISL toward this approach has been the signing of an MOU with AG&P Industrial to construct India’s first advanced modular EPC and fabrication facility in Andhra Pradesh.

This is essentially a gamble on the idea that future industrial construction projects will be awarded to contractors capable of constructing with factory-like accuracy and assembling at record speed. It’s also a gamble on the idea that these two things — factory-like manufacturing and assembling at speed — do not conflict with lifecycle costs.

# What Scale Actually Buys You

None of this works on theory; it must work in practice, in real projects and at real scale.

In excess of 16 million square feet delivered industrial portfolio from various sectors such as heavy engineering to warehousing, PISL’s team of over 600 has been faced with solving the problem of operation costs over and over again, in facilities with truly different load profiles and requirements.

This is an entirely different experience from that of a contractor who has only ever constructed one particular facility and is now trying to extrapolate the lessons learned from this experience.

# The Question Worth Asking Your Next EPC Partner

Before engaging any **industrial EPC contractor**, one should pose the tough question: how do they demonstrate the effect of their design decisions on reducing operating costs per square foot, and not only construction costs?

An ambiguous response to this question means that no life cycle calculations were made, and an ambiguous answer now becomes an exact amount that appears in utility bills in one to two years of operation.

Progressive, sustainable and durable – these are the criteria PISL applies to its own projects, and these are the criteria we would recommend applying to any **industrial EPC contractor** before putting capital in a facility which will be operated for the next two decades.

The right partner will not blink in the face of such a question. They will be ready to give an answer and even prove it by projects already implemented.

If you are considering building a new industrial facility and want to discuss how integrated EPC delivery would work in terms of your operating costs, PISL's specialists are ready to go through all the details project by project.

# A Few Questions Worth Putting to Any Bidder

In other words, how does a contractor measure life cycle savings versus simply making assertions about them?

The truth lies in quantifying energy usage, frequency of maintenance, and lifespan of equipment relative to the particular design being offered, rather than a vague assertion about efficient design.

Will utilising a single **industrial EPC contractor** be significantly more expensive than breaking down each aspect to multiple contractors?

Not necessarily, and more likely the converse, since an integrated team can eliminate the extra costs associated with overhead duplication and change orders that are common with multiple contractors managing separate scopes of work on the same project.

What information should you get in writing before agreeing to anything?

You should receive documentation of the areas in which value engineering was considered, energy performance assumptions behind the design, and maintenance access considerations that have been incorporated into the design.

# Build-to-Suit Industrial Facilities: Why Manufacturers Are Choosing Customised Infrastructure

Manufacturing infrastructure is no longer simply about finding an industrial building with enough space for production. As manufacturing processes become more specialised and global quality standards continue to evolve, businesses are increasingly looking for facilities that are designed around the way they actually operate.

Generic industrial facilities can provide a basic physical footprint, but they may not offer the right production flow, equipment integration, utility capacity, safety systems or expansion flexibility required by modern manufacturers.

This is where build-to-suit industrial facilities are becoming increasingly important. Instead of adapting operations to an existing building, manufacturers can develop infrastructure around their specific production requirements, creating facilities that support efficiency, compliance and long-term growth.

# Understanding Build-to-Suit Industrial Facilities

A build-to-suit industrial facility is a purpose-built manufacturing or industrial facility designed and constructed around the specific operational requirements of its future occupant.

Unlike speculative industrial buildings, which are generally developed with standard layouts and specifications to attract a broad range of tenants, build-to-suit facilities begin with the manufacturer's process requirements.

The production flow, machinery, material movement, storage requirements, employee movement, utilities, safety systems and future expansion plans can all be considered during the design stage.

This process-first approach allows the facility itself to become an extension of the manufacturing operation rather than simply a building that houses it.
![Industrial Infrastructure & Manufacturing1.avif](/images/blogs/Industrial_Infrastructure_and_Manufacturing1_80a8505b0d.avif)

For manufacturers investing in long-term operations, this distinction can have a significant impact on productivity, efficiency and the ability to adapt to future requirements.

# Why Manufacturers Are Moving Towards Customised Infrastructure

Manufacturing expectations have changed significantly. Companies operating in automotive, engineering, electronics, pharmaceuticals, industrial equipment and other specialised sectors increasingly need facilities that can meet demanding technical and operational requirements.

Global quality and compliance standards are also influencing facility design. Manufacturing plants may need specialised fire protection, environmental systems, controlled utilities, safety infrastructure and energy-efficient building services depending on the nature of production.

At the same time, manufacturing processes are becoming more specialised. Equipment layouts, automation systems, material handling and production lines need to work together efficiently. A generic building may require expensive modifications to accommodate these requirements.

Purpose-built infrastructure allows manufacturers to address these needs from the beginning.

A customised facility can also improve operational efficiency by reducing unnecessary movement of materials and people, supporting better production flow and creating more effective use of available space.

While the initial planning process for a build-to-suit facility may require greater coordination, the long-term benefits can outweigh the cost of adapting a generic facility. Better space utilisation, reduced operational bottlenecks, improved utility planning and easier future expansion can contribute to stronger lifecycle value.

The availability of industrial land and the development of new industrial zones are also creating opportunities for manufacturers to establish facilities that are aligned with their long-term expansion strategies.

# Benefits of Build-to-Suit Manufacturing Plants

The primary advantage of build-to-suit development is that the facility is designed around the operation rather than forcing the operation to fit an existing structure.
![Industrial Infrastructure & Manufacturing.avif](/images/blogs/Industrial_Infrastructure_and_Manufacturing_081f9bbb37.avif)

Production flow can be planned to minimise unnecessary movement between raw material storage, processing, assembly, quality control and finished goods dispatch.

Equipment integration can also be considered from the beginning. Structural systems, floor specifications, ceiling heights, equipment foundations, power requirements and material-handling systems can be coordinated with the production layout.

Safety and regulatory compliance are another important consideration. Fire protection, emergency access, ventilation, worker movement, hazardous-material handling and other safety requirements can be incorporated into the facility design instead of being added later.

Energy efficiency and sustainability can also be integrated at the planning stage. Building orientation, efficient MEP systems, lighting, ventilation, renewable energy integration and water-management systems can contribute to better environmental performance.

A purpose-built facility can further reduce operational bottlenecks and downtime by ensuring that infrastructure is aligned with production requirements.

Perhaps most importantly, the facility can be designed for future expansion. Additional production lines, warehouse capacity, utility requirements or new technologies can be considered before construction begins, helping manufacturers create infrastructure that can evolve with the business.

# Key Elements of Successful Build-to-Suit Facility Design

Successful build-to-suit development starts with understanding the manufacturing process.

A process-first planning approach allows architects, structural engineers, MEP specialists and manufacturing teams to work from a common understanding of how the facility will operate.

Structural design must reflect production requirements. Equipment loads, crane systems, machinery foundations, floor loading, clear heights and building spans may all influence the structural solution.

MEP engineering is equally important. Electrical distribution, HVAC, compressed air, process utilities, fire protection, water systems and other services must be coordinated with equipment and production requirements.

Utility planning should also consider both present and future requirements. Adequate capacity and infrastructure readiness can help avoid costly modifications when production expands.

Environmental and regulatory requirements need to be incorporated throughout the design and construction process. Depending on the project, these may include environmental clearances, fire and safety requirements, energy efficiency standards and other applicable regulations.

Future-proofing is another critical consideration. Manufacturers should evaluate how the facility can accommodate changes in production technology, additional equipment, increased capacity and evolving operational requirements.

The objective is not simply to build a facility that works today, but to create infrastructure that continues to support the business as it grows.

# The Role of EPC Expertise in Build-to-Suit Projects

Build-to-suit projects involve multiple disciplines and a high level of coordination. Engineering, procurement and construction therefore need to work together from the beginning.

An integrated EPC approach brings these functions under coordinated project management, helping maintain alignment between design intent, procurement decisions and site execution.

Single-point accountability can also simplify communication and decision-making. Instead of managing multiple independent parties, the client can work with an EPC partner responsible for coordinating the major project requirements.

This approach can help reduce project risks, improve schedule management and maintain quality throughout the project lifecycle.

For a manufacturing facility where production requirements directly influence the building design, maintaining alignment between engineering and construction is particularly important.

Every detail, from structural systems and utility infrastructure to equipment foundations and MEP coordination, needs to translate accurately from the design stage to physical execution.

# How Pragati Infra Solutions Limited Supports Build-to-Suit Development

Pragati Infra Solutions Limited has been delivering industrial and manufacturing infrastructure since 2009, with experience across sectors where precision, coordination and execution capability are critical.

PISL's experience includes automotive, engineering, warehousing and industrial manufacturing projects, giving the organisation an understanding of the different operational requirements that influence industrial facility development.

With more than 16 million square feet of delivered infrastructure and a multidisciplinary team of more than 600 professionals, PISL brings engineering, procurement and construction capabilities together under an integrated EPC approach.

This enables project requirements to be considered across the complete development lifecycle, from engineering and procurement through construction and delivery.

PISL's partnership with AG&P Industrial to establish an advanced modular EPC and fabrication facility in Andhra Pradesh further reflects its focus on modular, scalable and engineered industrial infrastructure.

For manufacturers looking to develop purpose-built facilities, this combination of industrial experience, multidisciplinary engineering and EPC execution provides a foundation for creating infrastructure designed around specific operational requirements.

The objective is not simply to deliver another industrial building. It is to create a facility that supports today's production requirements while remaining capable of adapting to tomorrow's growth.

# The Bottom Line

Manufacturing facilities are strategic assets that directly influence operational performance, productivity and long-term business growth.

Build-to-suit development allows manufacturers to align their physical infrastructure with their production processes, equipment requirements, compliance obligations and future expansion plans.

By considering these requirements from the beginning, purpose-built facilities can improve production flow, equipment integration, safety, energy efficiency and long-term scalability while reducing the limitations associated with generic industrial buildings.

The success of such a project ultimately depends on selecting the right development and EPC partner—one capable of translating operational requirements into practical engineering and delivering the facility with the required quality, coordination and schedule discipline.

# Industrial Corridors in India: New Growth Opportunities for Manufacturers and Developers

It is here that India is forging its future as an industrial nation in slow, steady strokes that link up ports and production centres and run through areas previously thought too far out of the loop for serious manufacturing investments.

This is India’s industrial corridor: a massive area of policy-driven development that is transforming where manufacturing is done, how manufactured goods move, and which areas will dominate India's economic landscape over the next three decades. For manufacturers looking for growth opportunities, developers looking for land opportunities, and EPC companies willing to play in such an arena, the stakes are high and the timing is critical.

![Industrial Corridors in India.avif](/images/blogs/Industrial_Corridors_in_India_7cff9486a8.avif)


Understand what the corridors can do for you and what building in them really means.

# What an Industrial Corridor Actually Is

It is a broad term; therefore, it is necessary to make it precise. For purposes of this discussion, an industrial corridor in the Indian context is not a road or a railway line. It is a development corridor that extends over hundreds of kilometres along a network of high-capacity transportation infrastructure designed to cluster manufacturing, logistics, and auxiliary industries.

An industrial corridor has an anchor that provides a platform for developing the corridor into an ecosystem for creating economic value through synergistic processes. In the case of the DMIC, it is the Western Dedicated Freight Corridor, which is a 1,500-km rail line designed to haul freight at very fast speeds between the two capitals, speeds that the current mixed traffic system cannot achieve.

Currently, there are five main industrial corridors in India: the Delhi-Mumbai IC, the Chennai-Bengaluru IC, the Amritsar-Kolkata IC, the Vizag-Chennai IC, and the Bengaluru-Mumbai EC. These corridors touch all regions in the country where manufacturing takes place.

# Why Manufacturing Growth Is Accelerating Here

The development of this infrastructure is no accident. It is a conscious policy response to several pressures that have fundamentally changed where global manufacturers choose to produce their goods.

With the China-plus-one diversification policy already underway in 2024 and growing geopolitical concerns, global corporations that used to produce their goods in one country have been forced to look for alternatives comparable in size, cost structure, and even infrastructure development. With its large internal market, growing talent pool of labourers, and government programs such as the PLI program, India ranks highly among such alternatives, especially in sectors such as electronics and semiconductors, defence components, and speciality chemicals.

However, it is not in the aspirations of global corporations to establish manufacturing operations. It is only with infrastructure development that they will decide. Electricity, fast freight services, ready-to-use industrial plots, and EPC companies capable of building facilities to international standards on an aggressive timeline are the factors.

The domestic industry is not staying behind either. With the advent of efficient logistics networks due to GST reforms, improved highway connectivity and access to large-scale industrial land in the vicinity of corridors, several capacity expansion plans have been made.

"India's industrial corridors are not just infrastructure projects. They are the architectural blueprint for where the country's manufacturing future will be built."

# The Logistics Infrastructure Equation

Growth in manufacturing and logistics infrastructure is not mutually exclusive; they come hand in hand, something that Indian industry policy has been oblivious to.

Multimodal Logistics Parks (MMLPs) being constructed within the node areas and the corridor network will enable last-mile delivery, intermodal movements, cold-chain management, and customs clearance through a single integrated park. The significance of this for manufacturers with logistical chains spanning several states cannot be overstated, which is true for most manufacturers in India.

The DFC, which forms the backbone of both DMIC and AKIC, is operational in substantial portions and has intangible benefits in freight time and reliability. A journey by rail that used to take four to five days now takes less than two days.

For developers, there is a constant demand pipeline for industrial and warehouse space created by the logistics infrastructure build-out. Each new factory unit in the corridor nodes creates upstream and downstream demand for storage and distribution. With each enhancement to the freight transportation system, the catchment area of logistics facilities expands. The fundamentals behind the industrial property market in corridor areas are, by design, solid.

# What It Takes to Build in These Zones and Why It Matters

A window of this size cannot be without its intricacies. Construction within an industrial corridor zone entails fulfilling a unique set of infrastructure needs, regulations, and delivery expectations that differ from those in a typical industrial build.

International standards must be met for construction, building services, and sustainability, given the increasing number of multinational tenants who won’t accept local specifications. Loading, fire safety, power, and effluent are assessed against global standards, not just code compliance.

There are deadlines and incentive schemes that include pricing, land stamp duty relief, and capex incentives, all tied to the start and completion dates. Missing out on these can cost a developer or manufacturer the money they thought they would make right from the beginning.

This is the kind of environment that makes choosing an EPC partner a critical decision.

# Where Pragati Infra Solutions Limited Fits Into This Picture

PISL has been providing extensive infrastructure in the country through various industrial complexes since 2009. And, the very sectors in which PISL has been operating for over 16 years are the sectors that drive the development of corridor zones.

With an expert workforce numbering over 600 people and a completed portfolio of over 16 million square feet of industrial structures, with expertise ranging from warehousing, automotive industries, heavy engineering, and industrial manufacturing, PISL provides the expertise required for a corridor-zone project. The EPC (Engineering, Procurement & Construction) model of one-stop responsibility for engineering, procurement, and construction is just what the client requires when timelines are stringent, specifications are non-negotiable, and the consequences of failure are expensive.

PISL's recent signing of an MOU (Memorandum of Understanding) with AG&P Industrial to establish the first-of-its-kind modular EPC and fabrication facility in Andhra Pradesh is a step in the right direction toward modular, scalable industrial infrastructure delivered through engineering expertise.

These industrial corridors represent a generational infrastructure play for investors. Companies in the manufacturing, development, and logistics sectors that take positions in these areas over the coming three to five years are setting themselves up for growth as the surrounding ecosystems evolve.

PISL is positioning itself for this and is willing to team up with companies that do so as well.

# How Smart Warehouses Are Transforming Supply Chain Efficiency in 2026

Consider when you ordered something online the other day, only to have it delivered the following morning. Did you give it much thought? Chances are, the reason for the seamless delivery is a warehouse that never sleeps, with robots transporting products at night, sensors monitoring the position of each pallet in real time, and algorithms predicting your order before you even open the app.

That is what a smart warehouse in 2026 looks like. For those industries that rely on precise supply chains, such as automotive, e-commerce, pharmaceuticals, or fast-moving consumer goods, the smart warehouse is no longer a competitive edge. It is a given.

The right question is: how does a warehouse become smart, and why is warehouse automation revolutionising supply chain management in its entirety?
![How Smart Warehouses Are Transforming Supply Chain Efficiency in 2026.avif](/images/blogs/How_Smart_Warehouses_Are_Transforming_Supply_Chain_Efficiency_in_2026_3bef2a8522.avif)

# From Storage Space to Intelligent Infrastructure

A traditional warehouse was a facility for storing goods until they were needed. It would use forklifts to move products. It used people to count the number of goods available. Everything would work just fine until something goes wrong, and it usually does at the most inconvenient point in time.

A smart warehouse starts viewing the whole process from a new angle. Rather than being a simple storage place, it becomes an active link in the supply chain, which can track its own inventory to the centimetre, interact with upstream suppliers and downstream logistics providers in real time, and optimise its operations without someone discovering a bottleneck.

All of the above is achieved through the integration of several technologies: IoT sensors installed across the warehouse, AGVs and AMRs moving materials, WMS software integrated with ERP solutions, and AI-powered tools for demand forecasting to avoid overstocking.

As a result, such a warehouse would have increased throughput, reduced the number of mistakes and lowered the cost per unit handled.

# What Warehouse Automation Actually Looks Like on the Ground

Talking about automation is one thing, but understanding how it really works when designed and implemented from scratch is another.

In the contemporary automated distribution centre, incoming goods are scanned and entered into the system without any data entry. With conveyor systems and AMRs, items are directed to storage locations determined by pick-frequency algorithms: high-frequency SKUs are stored near the dispatching point, while the rest are farther away. The incoming order creates a pick path, which will be performed by either robots or humans equipped with wearable devices in the most optimised manner.

All quality control checkpoints are automated. All dispatching processes are automated. And even the replenishment of stock at the picking points from the bulk storage areas is initiated automatically once the inventory falls below a certain level.

This brings many important advantages to supply chain management: order processing time is reduced from hours to minutes, the error rate approaches zero, and, more importantly, during peak loads, facility capacity can be increased without hiring more staff.

"The smartest warehouses being built today aren't just storage facilities. They are precision infrastructure engineered to think, adapt, and perform."

# Why 2026 Is a Turning Point

Discussion on smart warehouses has been going on for a decade now. Why, then, does 2026 look different?

For many reasons. Firstly, technology costs have reduced sufficiently that automation can be considered by mid-sized operators rather than just global giants. Autonomous Mobile Robot (AMR) platforms that once required multi-crore pilot projects are now available on a much smaller budget. Secondly, the Indian logistics landscape has matured enough, through the development of dedicated freight corridors, multimodal logistics parks, and supply chain rationalisation through GST, that the ecosystem now demands better-performing warehouses.

Thirdly, and most importantly, the post-pandemic realignment of supply chains is giving rise to the imperative of resilience in boardrooms. Companies that suffered months of lost business due to the shutdown of a single warehouse/supplier now have their sights set on building a robust, smart fulfilment network.

All of this means that we have before us a big construction and infrastructure opportunity that needs to be acted upon urgently. Smart warehouses should be built with automation in mind and not vice versa. In other words, decisions made during the design and construction of a warehouse will matter throughout its operational lifetime.

# Building Smart: Why the Construction Phase Matters

That is the area where most companies underestimate the challenges in achieving success. An intelligent warehouse is not a standard warehouse with a few robots. It is a custom-designed warehouse in which the architectural design, structural system, floor flatness tolerance, column layout, ceiling height, and MEP system are all designed with automation in mind from day one.

The floor flatness requirement is not trivial. Autonomous Mobile Robots (AMR) and Automated Storage systems require super-flat floors that comply with the FM2 or Super-Flat standards, which require far more construction experience than is usually required for a standard industrial floor. The column layout must be done based on the eventual rack layout and robot pathways. Power structure design must account for the loading profiles of automation equipment, charging stations, and data systems, which can differ greatly from those of conventional warehouses.

Making these considerations early in the construction phase is always cheaper than trying to fix them later. That is how one distinguishes good EPC partners from the others.

# How Pragati Infra Solutions Limited Approaches This Challenge

Since 2009, when Pragati Infra Solutions Limited began operations, warehousing projects have been an integral part of its portfolio. Over 16 years of operation and the completion of 16 million square feet of infrastructure projects, the organisation has developed warehouses in sectors where performance and precision are critical, including automotive, e-commerce, cold chain, and heavy industrial.

This experience has helped PISL gain a deeper understanding of the nature of warehouse development, which is more than civil construction. The 600-people-strong team at PISL consists of engineering experts specialising in structural, mechanical, and electrical engineering - the kind of expertise required for building a smart warehouse. PISL executes its projects under an EPC model, wherein a single party fully coordinates the design intent and execution.

As warehouse automation begins to revolutionise the way clients approach their warehousing requirements, PISL is well placed to deliver infrastructure that not only meets today's requirements but is also designed with the future automation needs of clients in mind.

And in 2026, a warehouse that cannot meet these requirements is not an asset; it is a liability waiting to be replaced.

Why Data Centre Construction Is Becoming India's Next Infrastructure Boom

A slow yet noticeable revolution seems to be underway within India's industrial real estate segment. Cranes are being put up in regions that weren't even considered five years ago. The speed of land tract acquisition in metro regions and Tier-II cities is comparable to the boom period experienced by commercial real estate over the last decade. All of this activity revolves around one common factor - data.

The Indian Data Centre Construction Industry has ceased to remain a small niche segment within the larger realm of industrial real estate. It has become one of the most critical infrastructure segments of the decade - an industry at the confluence of digital transformation, policy, and international investment flows. For EPC companies that recognise the intricacies of setting up such facilities, the upside potential is huge.

A Market That Is No Longer Speculative

For quite some time now, the development of data centres in India has been just a back-end necessity for telecom companies and a few big corporations. Times have changed; there is no going back.

![Data_Centre _&Digital Infrastructure.avif](/images/blogs/Data_Centre_and_Digital_Infrastructure_065af3faf6.avif)


Data centres saw more than 1 gigawatt of growth in India from 2020 to 2024. Experts estimate this will rise threefold by 2027. Places such as Mumbai, Chennai, Hyderabad, Pune, and Delhi-NCR are well-known data centres. However, data centres are not being built only in Tier-I locations. With cheaper land availability and improvements in power supply infrastructure, Tier-II cities are entering the game with government support.

What makes this happen? Here come three factors coming together: an exponential increase in mobile internet users, increased adoption of cloud services by Indian firms, and most importantly, AI infrastructure becoming available.

#AI Infrastructure Is Rewriting the Construction Brief

Traditional data centres were difficult to build. It required perfection in the way power was distributed, redundancy in the cooling system, a raised floor, structured cabling, and fire suppression, among other things, all done on a very short timeline and with a lot of attention to detail. The infrastructure used for AI technology has made this a much more difficult process.

AI workloads are dense on GPUs. While the power usage of one high-performance computing rack in an AI data centre can range from 30 to 100 kW, a traditional IT rack uses 5–10 kW. All the factors governing how a facility should be engineered have changed. Power density, cooling technology, load planning, and generator sizing are among the things that need to be revised.

For EPC contractors, this translates to the engineering of an intricate process. The civil, mechanical, and electrical engineers cannot work in silos. Precision is needed at every level, from substation design and transformer sizing to the positioning of cooling systems and even the commissioning of uninterruptible power systems.

## Industrial Projects of a Different Kind

It would be a gross oversimplification to regard data centre construction as just another specialised civil construction project. Indeed, on a grand scale, this type of project is nothing less than an all-encompassing industrial project, where logistics, supply chain management, and systems integration are equally complex as in an automotive manufacturing plant or in a major engineering works.

Just imagine all the work involved in constructing a hyperscale data centre: land preparation and civil works; high voltage power supply system; mechanical systems for cooling and environment control; fire fighting and detection systems; security infrastructure; fibre and backbone network integration, and finally commissioning that has to comply with tough uptime warranties before bringing a single server online.

The EPC delivery model of engineering, procurement, and construction, carried out under one umbrella, has become a more popular choice among data centre customers for good reasons.

## Policy Tailwinds and Private Capital

The Indian government has been an important catalyst in this regard. The Data Centre Policy Framework, the various incentives provided by state governments for data centre parks, and the wider Digital India program have ensured a positive environment for investment in this sector, both domestic and international.

Hyperscale giants such as Microsoft, Google, AWS, Meta, and many others have already made investments worth several billion dollars in India's data centre infrastructure over the next five years. The local players are aggressively scaling up their operations. The colocation facilities are growing at a much faster pace than ever before demanded by their booking requirements. The funds are available. Now the need is to execute this effectively.

## Where Pragati Infra Solutions Limited Stands

Construction of highly technical and sophisticated industrial facilities is an area of expertise in which PISL has been engaged since 2009. Over the years, PISL has successfully implemented large-scale EPC projects in industries that require the same level of proficiency and skill as data centres – precision engineering, tight timelines, multidisciplinary coordination, and the ability to deliver quality in large quantities.

With over 600 personnel, a project portfolio exceeding 16 million square feet, and experience across multiple industries, including warehousing, automotive, heavy engineering, and industrial manufacturing, PISL boasts capabilities that perfectly match those required for a data centre.

PISL's latest agreement with AG&P Industrial to develop India's first-ever advanced modular EPC & fabrication facility in the state of Andhra Pradesh is another signal of PISL's willingness to push the boundaries of large-scale project implementation in India through EPC. This very capability - modular, scalable, and precise is exactly what is needed in a partner by the data centre industry.

Progressive. Innovative. Sustainable. Limitless. These are not merely PISL's brand values. They are exactly the approach needed to construct data centres in their purest form.

## Sustainability Is Not Optional Anymore

With more data centres popping up in India, there is now more focus on the resources they require. It takes just one hyperscale data centre to match the electricity consumption of an entire town and use a million litres of water per year for cooling purposes. The growing ESG standards and the introduction of energy efficiency standards by regulatory bodies in India have made sustainability a must-have design parameter rather than a bonus one.

It means that each of the steps of data centre construction should consider sustainability, from designing energy-efficient building envelopes to installing renewable power sources and creating cooling systems based on water recycling and waste management solutions. Green building certification systems such as LEED and IGBC will need to be adhered to. In other words, for engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) partners, it is necessary to consider sustainability as a factor at par with power density and load.

And it is here that the choice of the right construction partner comes into play. Sustainability is not just a buzzword in PISL’s business approach but one of the core principles applied to every major construction project in India.

## The Bottom Line

The development of data centres is the next big infrastructure segment for India, and it is coming in full force, not incrementally.

With a robust pipeline of data centre projects fuelled by demand generated by the application of artificial intelligence, investment by hyperscalers, government support, and digitisation, the task of constructing India's data centre infrastructure presents an exciting challenge for companies with the right skill set.

This is not a question of whether India's data centre infrastructure will be built, but rather of who will build it.
